extracted.intended_audience: readers/students interested in Aristotle's Poetics and Great Books (general literature students and humanities readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and interpreting the key teachings and evaluative principles in Aristotle's Poetics about poetry (especially tragedy, epic, and comedy) and what makes them effective. Geared toward readers seeking a concise guide to Aristotle's criteria for poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic art as natural organic activity (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic art (poieses) is a natural organic activity and an imitative act (mimesis); it is also a kind of reflection of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats poetry as emerging naturally because humans imitate from childhood and delight in imitations. Poetry arises along with harmony and rhythm; imitation is fundamental to the origin and practice of poetic arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of poetry must be distinguished
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is divided into kinds: epic poetry, tragedy, comedy, and dithyrambic poems (a kind of Dionysian choral hymn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding a poem requires identifying its kind, since each kind has different objects, means, and rules (e.g., epic vs. tragedy vs. comedy). Examples: Homer (epic), Aeschylus and Sophocles (tragedy), Aristophanes (comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: serious vs inferior characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance art imitates people who are either of a serious moral stature (better people) or a lower moral stature (inferior people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy generally imitates people 'better than we are' (noble figures), while comedy imitates inferior people. This distinction helps determine tone, subject-matter, and moral orientation of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should represent the ridiculous as harmless
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of a lower sort of people; 'what is ridiculous is a part of what is ugly' — the ridiculous is a kind of missing the mark that is painless and not destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic elements should ridicule or present absurdity without causing real harm; examples include masks and harmless ridicule. Aristotle notes comedy's origins (Sicily) and links comedic meter (iambic) to the practice of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and natural causes of poetic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic forms arose from natural human imitation, delight in imitation, and from rhythmic and harmonic practices; specific forms (e.g., tragic or comic) have particular historical origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: iambic meter arose from ridicule, tragic art from phallic songs and satyr-plays; innovations (adding actors, scenery, speaking) shaped the evolution of forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's purpose: arouse fear and pity to achieve katharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy accomplishes its end by means of fear and pity, and cleanses these states of feeling through katharsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful tragedy must evoke appropriate emotional responses (pity and fear) and resolve them in a purgative or clarifying way for the audience — this is central to tragic art's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: The six constituent parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has six parts: story (imitation of the action/plot), states of character (characters), wording (diction), thinking (thought), spectacle, and song-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These six parts are the dimensions by which a tragedy can be analyzed and evaluated; plot is primary among them but diction, thought, spectacle, and song contribute to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot unity and completeness (beginning, middle, end; single whole action)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be a complete whole with a beginning, middle, and end; it is an imitation of one whole action (with magnitude), not merely a collection of episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots should show a coherent build-up and resolution; even when containing small side-stories (as in the Odyssey), the central action must remain unified. Unity and magnitude are marks of the highest poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia) and discovery (anagnorisis) as plot devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragedy draws the soul by means of reversals and discoveries; discovery is leading from ignorance to recognition. A tragedy is best when a discovery and a reversal happen at the same time (as in Oedipus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective plotting employs these devices to transform the audience’s understanding and to intensify emotional impact; simultaneous reversal+recognition is the ideal configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering as a key element
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffering is the third and key element of tragedy (alongside reversal and discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of genuine suffering in the action contributes to the cathartic effect and the seriousness (magnitude) appropriate to tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot plausibility: 'what is likely' over strict necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes 'what is likely' versus 'what is necessary'; the likely sequence is an imitation of human action working itself out — plots should be probable rather than mechanically necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plausibility preserves the possibility of twists and moral/psychological development; a plot that unfolds only by necessity leaves little room for meaningful recognition or reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic/random (inferior) plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: An inferior poet will create an episodic story; this is inferior because it is random. The highest form of poetics is orderly and harmonized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should be organized around causal and thematic cohesion rather than a sequence of unrelated episodes; coherence marks higher artistic achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character requirements for tragedy (reliability and moral position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in the play should be solidly reliable; tragedy ought not to showcase a decent man going from good to bad fortune through vice, nor show bad characters becoming good as that is least tragic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic hero should be neither supremely virtuous nor utterly villainous; the fall should come from a 'missing of the mark' (tragic error) rather than from moral depravity — this preserves pity and avoids repulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia / 'missing the mark' as cause of misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic misfortune often arises from some 'missing of the mark' (sometimes called the 'tragic mistake' or hamartia), not from simple vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concept explains how an otherwise respectable or relatable character can suffer catastrophe in a way that generates pity and avoids moral condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs. tragedy: narration vs performance and shared elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry is similar to tragedy in dealing with serious subjects and magnitude, but epic uses narration while tragedy uses performance; parts of epic are mostly contained within tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating epic or tragedy, note differences of medium (narration vs staged action) even as they share concerns like magnitude and imitation of serious actions; Homer is credited with the peak of epic, tragedians later perfected tragic art.
